processing: As with other Wuyi named bushes, picked and made separately as a rock oolong: partly oxidised, rolled and roasted.
harvest_season: Typical of Wuyi rock teas, a single spring picking; no specific timing is recorded for this bush.
appearance_dry: Twisted dark strips, as is usual for roasted Wuyi oolong.
appearance_liquor: Orange-amber, typical of a medium-roast rock tea.
appearance_wet: As with other rock teas, broad leaves with darkened edges.
taste_profile: No settled tasting description exists; expect the roast and mineral body common to Wuyi rock teas.

brewing.notes: Standard rock-tea brewing: near-boiling water and short steeps in a small vessel.

vintage_note: Sold like other Wuyi rock teas, by the year of the spring harvest and usually after the roast has rested. It is a rare name in the trade, so ask what bush and place stand behind it.
description:
Bu Jian Tian means does not see the sky. It is a Wuyi named bush, and its name belongs to the group that describes where the plant grows rather than its leaf, shape or scent. Whether it refers to one specific sheltered spot is not established.

Named bushes are picked and made apart from ordinary garden leaf, in the general way of rock oolongs. Nothing further about this tea's making is recorded.

Brew it hot and fast like other rock teas. Tasting notes in print are scarce, so go in with an open mind rather than a list of flavours.

A romantic name is easy to put on any bag of Wuyi tea. A seller who can tell you the year, the roast and the growing area deserves more trust than one who only tells you the story.
history: Bu Jian Tian appears in Chinese accounts of Wuyi tea among the bushes named for their growing environment. Its selection, age and original location are not established.
